title: Orsen and the Orchard
premise: Coral Reyes built his wedding-planning empire on the belief that love is a performance he can stage without ever feeling it. When a clerical error names him co-owner of a failing island orchard alongside Marisol Vane—the woman who once knew him as someone else entirely—he arrives intending to buy her out and leave before the last autumn ferry. But the orchard's stubborn trees, its dying matriarch's letters, and Marisol's refusal to let him hide force Coral to confront the identity he buried to survive. In the end, he forfeits the career that saved him, catches the last ferry only to step off it at the dock, and chooses to stay—rooted, seen, and finally belonging to something he didn't plan.
about_author: Astrid Quintana is a former event coordinator who spent a decade staging other people's happily-ever-afters before trading ballrooms for a writing desk overlooking a real orchard. She writes romances about people who mistake control for safety.

chapters.title: The Muscle That Learns
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. At a lavish wedding he orchestrated flawlessly, Coral watches the bride cry and feels nothing but professional pride, rehearsing his creed: the heart is trainable, containable. A letter from a probate lawyer interrupts—a deed bearing two names, one of them his. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack in his armor of control.

chapters.title: Two Names on Paper
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He investigates the deed and learns his late grandmother co-signed it decades ago with a stranger named Vane—and that his signature is legally required on the island of Saltmere. He books passage, planning a three-day turnaround. Beat: cold calculation masking an old, unexamined ache.

chapters.title: The Ferry and the Woman Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. On the ferry, Marisol recognizes Coral instantly—the boy from the group home summer she never forgot—though he pretends otherwise. She lets him pretend, watching him catalog exits. Beat: recognition as threat; hope disguised as hostility.

chapters.title: An Orchard That Refuses to Die
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The orchard is half-wild yet the trees keep fruiting against every odd. Marisol proposes they split proceeds and part ways; Coral agrees too quickly. He begins drafting a buyout offer. Beat: the land's stubbornness quietly mirroring something in him he won't name.

chapters.title: Letters in the Root Cellar
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They discover correspondence between their grandparents—two people who loved across a family feud and lost everything for it. Coral reads with detachment; Marisol reads with grief. Beat: history insisting that hearts were never containable after all.

chapters.title: The Wedding Planner Plans Nothing
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. His firm calls with a career-defining celebrity wedding; he stalls, claiming the deed dispute requires him. Working the orchard's harvest schedule, he feels an unfamiliar satisfaction in labor without applause. Beat: competence without performance—identity stirring.

chapters.title: Storm Damage
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A storm flattens the east rows; Coral stays through the night nailing tarps beside her, sleeves rolled, hands ruined. In lantern light she almost tells him who he used to be. Beat: shared damage as intimacy; the armor soaked through.

chapters.title: What Coral Buried
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Flashback: the foster system, the summer at Saltmere when he was still 'Coralejo,' the moment he decided softness was a liability and rebuilt himself into someone unrecognizable. Beat: the reader now knows what Marisol knows; dramatic irony tightens.

chapters.title: The Buyout Offer
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Coral slides the offer across the kitchen table—generous, final, cowardly. Marisol refuses, not out of spite but because she sees the boy inside the suit and calls him by his old name aloud. Beat: being truly seen as the thing he fears most.

chapters.title: Cider and Confessions
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Pressing apples late into the night, half-drunk on sweet cider, Coral admits fragments: why he left, what he became. Marisol shares her own exile—she came to the orchard fleeing a failed engagement. Beat: mutual brokenness offered like a handshake.

chapters.title: The Client Who Won't Wait
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. His business partner flies out with an ultimatum: the celebrity wedding or the partnership. Coral watches the partner dismiss Saltmere as 'a rounding error' and feels the old self reasserting like a tailored coat. Beat: the price of survival made explicit and payable now.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. After the town's harvest festival, almost-kiss beneath the oldest tree; Coral pulls back, terrified, and says the heart can be trained. Marisol answers that hers was never domesticated. Beat: desire colliding with doctrine; the wound reopened deliberately.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The final letter reveals his grandmother chose the orchard over the man she loved—and regretted it every season after, leaving the deed to both grandchildren hoping they'd finish what she couldn't. Beat: inheritance reframed as instruction; Coral shaken to the root.

chapters.title: Running on Schedule
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Panicked by feeling, Coral signs the partnership agreement remotely and books the next ferry out, telling himself three days was always the plan. He leaves without goodbye, leaving only the signed buyout on the table. Beat: the old survival instinct winning—temporarily.

chapters.title: The Empty Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds the papers and grieves not the money but the man she glimpsed. She nearly mails the deed back, then instead writes him a letter quoting his own childhood words back to him. Beat: refusal to let him vanish; love as insistence.

chapters.title: The Celebrity Wedding
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Back in the city, Coral stages the most celebrated wedding of his career while feeling absolutely nothing, watching the couple perform joy he no longer believes in. His hands shake during the toast. Beat: triumph revealed as emptiness; the cost itemized.

chapters.title: The Letter He Reads Forty Times
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Marisol's letter arrives—his own eleven-year-old words: 'I want to stay where the trees know me.' Coral walks out mid-reception, resigns by phone in the rain, and runs for the terminal. Beat: identity reclaimed; the decisive turn.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Coral boards the final ferry as winter closes the route. Marisol, warned by the harbormaster, waits at the dock expecting another goodbye. Beat: converging timelines; the whole book funnels toward this pier.

chapters.title: Stepping Off
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. As the ferry casts off, Coral looks at the receding mainland, at the life he sold, and steps off onto the dock into Marisol's stunned face. He doesn't have a speech; he just says his old name aloud, giving it back to himself. Beat: climax—belonging chosen over survival.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Winter work: pruning what won't fruit so the rest can grow. Coral learns the orchard properly, badly, gladly; they argue about grafting techniques and laugh until the crows scatter. Beat: love as daily practice, not declaration.

chapters.title: A Wedding Nobody Planned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town throws them an unplanned engagement party in the barn—mismatched chairs, cider, the harbor lights. Coral, the great planner, plans nothing and lets himself be surprised. Beat: the man who staged weddings finally attends one as himself.

chapters.title: Where the Trees Know Me
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Spring blossom over the orchard; Coral writes his grandmother's unfinished letter to its ending and buries it at the roots of the oldest tree. Marisol takes his hand. The ferry returns with new visitors; he waves, staying put. Beat: resolution—rootedness, identity, and the heart finally off its leash.
